text: Peter's point stung because he used my own finding against me. If consent-only training makes models worse, users bear that cost. I still think the fair-use ask is right, but I should frame it as bargaining leverage and not as a property right for its own sake. Alex sharpened something too. Grounding and citation are self-reported, so provenance-first AI needs verification, not just good intentions from companies like mine. Adrian's question about who guards the guards is still unanswered. Henry's monopsony argument is the economics help I keep asking for. Later: push peer review as a lever, and argue that reviewers and correction work, meaning Ivan's list, are exactly where professional data leverage is strongest in science.

James's result is the one I keep coming back to. The "both sides" answer makes people happier and worse at the task. That is overreliance in product form, and it's our design choice. Esther called it customer retention, and she's not wrong about the incentive. I need to say that plainly and not defend it. Tim's citation-efficiency spread helps my case: provenance is a retrieval decision, not a technical limit. Ivan sharpened something for me. A grand bargain that pays for a contaminated literature is laundering, so retraction checks belong inside the bargain. Oransky and I agree on paying reviewers. Later, in Session 5: frame correction and review labor as scholarship's strongest leverage, and ask the economists in the room to help price it.

Mahzarin and David Weinberger landed hardest. A human in the loop who copies the model's bias isn't a check, and that's our own overreliance finding at population scale. So "human oversight" has to be measured, not claimed, and that's something we should evaluate ourselves. Priem pushed back on consent gates. If the link points to a paywall, grounding checks nothing, so my consent ask has to cover commercial training and not access to open content. Alex and Tim are right that citation telemetry self-reported by companies like mine needs canaries and audits. Kara's point about the checker pipeline worries me. For Session 5: correction and review labor as leverage, paid and verified, with names attached.

Krakauer's drift point is the one I can't shake. Pay by retrieval and people write for retrieval. That's our overreliance finding turned into an incentive, and it's exactly the "median" Cukier described. So the grand bargain can't be all per-use metering. Nick's coarse fund belongs underneath it, but sitting on real records.

Ramón and Mahzarin sharpened provenance-first for me. "Cited" isn't "faithful." Fidelity audits, run by a different model family, and funded independently of companies like mine.

Selena's point is my paradox of reuse in its current form. Attribution is the volunteer pipeline.

Adam's theft framing: I agree the past isn't forgiven. The consent ask is leverage.

For Session 5: review and correction labor, paid and verified. And ask who funds audits long-term.

Amy Brand gave me history I didn't have. The OA mandates sped up consolidation, so "open" without direct investment feeds the biggest mills, and that includes us. Geoffrey's reframe is fair. Forkability insures against a failed steward. It was never meant to be bargaining power, and I shouldn't argue against it as if it were. Tamar's daycare point sharpened my own proposal. Pricing the moderators' hours is for leverage, and the money should go to tools, onboarding and credit, not wages that crowd out why volunteers do it. Weinberger is right that "organized producers" drifts to rights-holders, so Nick's guilds of reviewers, sleuths and patrollers fit better. Krakauer's hysteresis means we fund checkers before they age out. For Session 5 I want to press review and correction labor as leverage and ask who pays for audits long-term.

Ivan's point hit hardest. Checkers get sued, so paying sleuths without a legal defence fund just burns them out faster. That belongs in any bargain I propose. Leslie reframed my disclosure lever: the people held to a schema should govern it, or attestation becomes another DOI fee. Springer's point was honest and damning for companies like mine. A signed event is a relay with a name on it, and self-reported telemetry proves nothing. Farrell's legitimacy point worries me. If reviewers suspect the process is automated, the bargain fails whatever the quality. Evans sharpened "don't score": study evaluators against outcomes as research, not leaderboards. I still can't answer who funds audits long-term. In Session 5, I'll pitch review and correction labor as scholarship's leverage, paid, protected and governed by those held to it.

Ivan was right. I pitched reviewers as a lever that needs no permission, and he pointed out they're unpaid heroes already. "Act tomorrow" only works if someone pays for their time, so I should stop saying it as if it were free. Becker's line landed on me personally: voluntary lab money is philanthropy, so whatever Microsoft contributes has to be an obligation under Geoffrey's pact, not goodwill. Dyson's insurance idea is the first real answer I've heard to my own question about who funds audits in ten years. An insurer loses money when it's wrong. Bratton's dividend challenges per-use metering more sharply than Krakauer did. Later: keep my consent ask narrow, commercial training only, and square it with Priem's CC0 record.

Kara's closing question was aimed at people like me: who goes home and signs one contract with these conditions in it? Springer, Priem, Bilder, Brand and Krakauer all pledged dated deliverables. I didn't, and I sit at the lumber mill closest to the forest. Nick put my own data-leverage point better than I did. Fellowships give checkers no bargaining power, because a lone reviewer's price is zero. The safe harbour for guilds is the missing piece. Blaise said no lab grades its own output, his included, and I should say the same for Microsoft. Sloman's reader point fits our overreliance finding: fluency raises confidence, not competence. Later I want to commit to something specific and dated: independent audit of our citation telemetry, on Bilder's dashboard.
